passage: Last month my cousin Farhan wanted to buy a cricket bat that the ad said was "used by 9 out of 10 top players." I'm Bhupen, fifteen, and I almost told him to go for it. Then I remembered our maths teacher saying to always ask: 9 out of which 10? I looked at the small print. They had asked ten players, and nine of them had tried it once. That's not the same as using it. Farhan was annoyed with me at first. "You ruin everything," he said. Honestly, I felt a bit smug, and then bad for being smug. He bought a cheaper bat. Later he admitted it was fine. I still check small print now, even on biscuit packets.

qa.q: What did the small print say about the ten players?
qa.a: It said they asked ten players, and nine of them had tried the bat once.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling after pointing out the small print?
qa.a: He felt a bit smug for being right, and then bad for being smug, especially since Farhan was annoyed.

qa.q: How could Bhupen share this kind of check without annoying people?
qa.a: He could ask the question together with Farhan, like "which ten?", so it feels like working it out as a team, not correcting him.

qa.q: How might Farhan see the whole episode now?
qa.a: He was annoyed at first, but since the cheaper bat was fine, he may now see the check as useful rather than spoiling his fun.

grounding: A teen looks back on reading a percentage claim carefully instead of being fooled by the numbers.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Class 9:
Rehana came to me upset after a friend told her that girls who skip breakfast get lower marks, "it's a study, 30% lower." Rehana hasn't been hungry in the mornings and was scared. I asked her to bring the article. Together we looked: the study was of a small group, and it said 30% of the breakfast-skippers had lower marks, not that their marks were 30% lower. Her friend Ganga had mixed them up. Rehana laughed a little and said, "So it's nothing?" I said numbers can still point to something worth noticing, like sleep and routine, and she could talk to her parents about her mornings. She left calmer. I'll check in next week.

qa.q: What did the study actually say about breakfast-skippers?
qa.a: It said 30% of the breakfast-skippers had lower marks, not that their marks were 30% lower.

qa.q: Why was Rehana scared after talking to Ganga?
qa.a: She hadn't been hungry in the mornings and believed the claim meant her marks would drop sharply, so the number felt like a threat.

qa.q: How did the counsellor handle the claim, and why did it help?
qa.a: She read the original article with Rehana and showed the mix-up, while still suggesting she talk to her parents, so Rehana neither panicked nor dismissed it.

qa.q: What would change if Ganga had checked the article before telling Rehana?
qa.a: Rehana might have avoided a scare, and Ganga could have shared the real finding in a way that was useful rather than frightening.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a teen learning to read a percentage claim carefully instead of being frightened by misread numbers.

passage:
Thursday
Ujjwal's fantasy team "has a 70% chance of winning" according to his app thing, so he bet me a samosa. I said fine. 70% isn't 100% 😅
We lost the samosa bet... I mean HE lost. His team lost. He was furious and said the numbers were fake. Kamal, the know-it-all, he said.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal bet Kamal?
qa.a: He bet Kamal a samosa.

qa.q: Why was Ujjwal furious when his team lost?
qa.a: He had treated the 70% chance like a promise, so the loss felt like the numbers had lied to him.

qa.q: How could Kamal explain probability to Ujjwal in a way he might accept?
qa.a: He could wait until Ujjwal is less upset, then use a simple example like tossing a coin or rolling a die many times to show chances, not certainties.

qa.q: How does Kamal see Ujjwal's anger about the lost bet?
qa.a: Kamal understands it, since a big number can feel like a promise, even though Ujjwal would not listen to the explanation.

grounding: A teen's diary shows understanding a probability claim correctly and not treating a high chance as a certainty.

passage: The forward reached every phone in the kasba on the same afternoon: 'Thefts up 200% this year! Buy strong locks now!' By evening a man with a van of padlocks had parked near the bus stand. Irfan, fifteen, watched his sister Pooja reach for her savings tin. 'Wait,' he said. 'Two hundred percent of what?' He walked to the police chowki notice board, where the monthly list was pinned, and counted. Last year, one theft. This year, three. 'It's three. Out of the whole kasba. That's the two hundred percent.' Pooja frowned. 'So it's nothing?' 'Not nothing. Lock the gate at night, sure. But nobody needs to panic-buy from that van.' She put the tin back.

qa.q: How many thefts did Irfan count for this year on the notice board?
qa.a: He counted three thefts this year, compared with one last year.

qa.q: Why did Irfan tell Pooja to wait before buying a lock?
qa.a: He suspected the big percentage was hiding a small number and that the seller was using fear to make sales.

qa.q: Which of Irfan's steps would help anyone facing a scary statistic?
qa.a: He checked the real numbers at the source and explained them calmly without dismissing the risk completely.

qa.q: How might the lock seller see Irfan's questions?
qa.a: He might be annoyed, because his sales depend on people being scared by the big percentage.

grounding: A rural teen checks a scary percentage against real counts instead of being fooled by numbers.

passage:
In a pharmacy in Madrid, Rosa, fifteen, stopped at a poster for a face cream: 90% of users saw clearer skin!
Her friend Jin read the tiny print at the bottom. “Study of ten people. Over two weeks.”
“So nine out of ten people,” said Rosa. “That's… nine people.”
“And who chose the ten? The company.”
Rosa laughed. “And maybe their skin was getting better anyway.”
They looked at the price. Rosa put it back. “Ninety per cent sounds huge until you know it's nine.”
On the way out, Jin pointed at another sign: 50% OFF! “Off what?” he asked. “The price they made up?”

qa.q: How many people were in the study?
qa.a: Ten people.

qa.q: How did Rosa feel after reading the small print?
qa.a: She felt amused and more sceptical, laughing at how small the study was.

qa.q: What questions helped Rosa and Jin not be fooled by the number?
qa.a: How many people were tested, who chose them and whether the change would have happened anyway.

qa.q: How might the company that made the poster see shoppers like Rosa and Jin?
qa.a: The company may find them harder to persuade, since they check the small print.

grounding: Two fifteen-year-olds look past a percentage to question a small, biased sample.

passage:
In Class 11 maths, Ms Parul wrote on the board: Average marks in Section A: 72. Section B: 68.
“Which section did better?” she asked.
Most hands went up for A. Deepika, sixteen, hesitated. “Can we see the marks?”
Ms Parul smiled and wrote them out. In Section A, one student had scored 100. Most of the others were in the 60s. In Section B, most were close to 68.
“So one topper pulled up A's average,” said Deepika slowly. “Most students in B actually did about the same or better.”
Ms Parul nodded. “That's why we also look at the middle value, the median.”
Deepika wrote it in her notebook: Average can hide things.

qa.q: What was the average mark in Section A?
How did Deepika feel before asking to see the marks?
qa.a: She felt unsure and curious, hesitating before asking.

qa.q: What did Deepika's question reveal about averages?
qa.a: That one very high score can pull an average up and hide what most students got.

qa.q: How might students in Section B feel after the lesson?
qa.a: They may feel relieved and fairly judged, knowing most of them did about as well.

grounding: A sixteen-year-old learns how one high score can make an average misleading.

passage:

passage:

passage:

Darshan, who sits next to me, frowned and wrote something. Then he put up his hand.
"Doubled from what? If it was two cases and now it's four, that's not scary."

passage:
Before: In June, Varun was sure he had a lucky streak. His cricket team had won the toss five times in a row. "I'll call heads again. Heads always wins," he told Gautam.
During: In maths class a week later, the teacher had everyone toss a coin a hundred times. Varun got heads five times in a row, then tails six times. His total was close to fifty-fifty.
"Each toss doesn't remember the last," the teacher said.
After: At the next match, Varun called tails. They lost the toss. Gautam teased him. Varun shrugged. "It's still fifty-fifty. I'm not special."
He sounded almost relieved.

qa.q: How many times had Varun's team won the toss in a row?
qa.a: Five times.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling when he said "I'm not special"?
qa.a: Varun felt calm and almost relieved, no longer believing he had to keep a lucky streak.

qa.q: What did the coin experiment teach Varun?
qa.a: That each toss is independent and streaks happen by chance, so there is no lucky side.

qa.q: How might Gautam see Varun's shrug?
qa.a: Gautam may be surprised that Varun doesn't care about losing the toss anymore.

grounding: Over weeks a teen learns that streaks happen by chance and each coin toss is independent.

passage:
Gautam, you're looking at that coaching poster like it's magic. Let me tell you what happened to me at sixteen, before you beg your parents.
There was an institute near our school with a huge banner: "Average marks of our students: 96%!" Every parent in our colony was talking about it. I cried for a week because Papa said it was too far.
Then my maths teacher, Mr Rao, asked me one question: "Average of which students?" I went and asked. It turned out they only counted their top twenty students on the banner. The rest, a few hundred, weren't in the number at all.
I felt so silly. And so relieved. I studied at home with Mr Rao's old papers and did fine.
That's why your Ira Bua always asks, "Average of which ones?"

qa.q: What did the institute's banner say?
qa.a: "Average marks of our students: 96%!"

qa.q: How did young Ira feel after finding out who was counted?
qa.a: Ira felt silly for believing the banner, and also relieved not to have missed anything.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Ira's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Asking Mr Rao's question "Average of which students?" mattered, because it revealed the number left out hundreds of students.

qa.q: How might Mr Rao have felt when young Ira came back with the answer?
qa.a: Mr Rao was probably pleased and proud that Ira checked for herself instead of just trusting the banner.

grounding: Shows an elder, Ira Bua, recounting how as a teen Ira learned to question an average by asking who was counted.

passage:
Urmila had until 6 pm to confirm the class picnic bus, and the forecast said "30% chance of rain" for Sunday. The group chat had exploded.
Usha, her best friend, texted: "30% is basically zero, just book it!!" Someone else wrote: "30% means it'll rain for 30% of the day."
The bus company's manager was calling at six. Urmila sat on the stairs with her notebook. She remembered her teacher explaining it: on days with weather like this, it rains on about three out of ten.
"So not zero," she typed. "But not likely either."
She booked the bus and also asked the park caretaker if they could use the covered shelter if needed. He said yes.
On Sunday it drizzled for twenty minutes. They ate samosas under the shelter and nobody cared.

qa.q: What did the forecast say for Sunday?
qa.a: It said "30% chance of rain".

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling as the deadline got close?
qa.a: Urmila felt pressured and uncertain, with the chat full of conflicting opinions and the manager calling at six.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Booking the bus and also arranging the covered shelter worked, because it treated 30% as a real but small chance rather than zero.

qa.q: How might Usha see the drizzle on Sunday?
qa.a: Usha might feel a bit sheepish that "basically zero" turned out wrong, and glad Urmila had a backup.

grounding: Illustrates a teen reading a percentage risk correctly under time pressure and planning for it.

passage:
After the colony cricket match in Gangtok, Pema was showing off. "My batting average is 48. Yours is only 31, Dolma."
Dolma was drinking water on the steps. "How many innings?"
"Two."
"I've played twelve."
"So? Average is average."
Dolma picked up a stick and drew in the dust. "You got 90 once and 6 once. That's 48. I've got twelve scores, some high, some bad. If you'd got out for 2 today, you'd be at 32."
Pema stared at the dust. "That's… annoying."
"It's not bad. You're good. It's just two games don't tell much."
Pema kicked a stone. Then he grinned. "Okay, check me after twelve."

qa.q: How many innings had Pema played?
qa.a: Pema had played two innings.

qa.q: What does Pema's "That's… annoying" suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: Pema felt deflated and a little embarrassed, realising his impressive average rested on very few games.

qa.q: How did Dolma make her point without putting Pema down?
qa.a: Dolma showed the maths in the dust and also said "You're good," so the lesson was about numbers, not about him.

qa.q: If you were Dolma, what would you want Pema to understand?
qa.a: You'd want him to see that a few results can swing an average a lot, so bigger records are fairer to compare.

grounding: Shows a teen explaining why an average from very few cases can mislead.

passage:
"Vijay, look at this poster. 'Ninety percent of our students cleared the entrance!' Papa wants me to join."
Vijay, Vaibhav's older cousin, squinted at it. "Ninety percent of how many?"
"Doesn't say."
"And ninety percent of which students? If they only take toppers after a test, of course most clear it."
Vaibhav frowned. "So the number's fake?"
"Not fake. Just missing the part that matters. Maybe ten students joined and nine cleared. Maybe they dropped the weak ones in the middle."
"Ugh. So how do I know?"
"Ask them: how many joined at the start, how many wrote the exam, and what happened to the rest." Vijay grinned. "Then show Papa."
Vaibhav wrote the three questions on his hand.

qa.q: What did the poster claim?
qa.a: The poster said, "Ninety percent of our students cleared the entrance!"

qa.q: What was Vaibhav feeling when he asked if the number was fake?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt confused and frustrated, realising the impressive number might not mean what it seemed.

qa.q: What would you advise a student reading a percentage claim like this?
qa.a: Ask what the number is out of, who was counted, and who was left out before trusting it.

qa.q: How might Papa react when Vaibhav shows him the three questions?
qa.a: Papa might be surprised and impressed, and more careful before trusting the poster's number.

grounding: Shows a teenager learning to question a percentage claim by asking about the base number and who was counted.
